title: How high and low the trombone played
summary: Dutcher asks what share of the notes were above or below F. Ridgley says about half, and he preferred playing higher near the trumpet rather than imitating a bass.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Would you say that most of the time, when you didn't have the melody line, the trombone music was going to be playing, most of the time would you be playing your notes below middle B flat or would you be, say, up to F above B flat quite a bit?
Most of the time, up to F. Up to F. Yeah, F.
What percentage would you say of the music was between F and F and then what percentage was below F?
Well, now you're gutting that percentage, but now I don't know what it's going to be.
What part? Half, would you say half?
I see. Because when you tell me that boom, boom, ba-ba-boom, boom, boom, boom, I always think of that as way down and say, way below F, you know, boom in the bass part.
You could, yeah, half above the staff. Yeah. Yeah. Oh yeah, that's mostly that stuff is…
Well, I mean F in the staff, the second note, you know, second line of the bass.
I don't know, bass is the full line. I mean? Bass chord, F. F is the full line. I'd be… Well, I'm thinking of the bass… Yeah, that's right.
F is the fourth line, he counts it. Well, the fourth line, I was calling you second down. That's right, you count from the bottom, don't you?

Yeah, fourth to the bottom. Right, fourth line up. Well, speaking of that F, what part of your, what part of the notes that you would play, non-melody, would be below that? Most of it or half of it or what would you say? I don't quite understand. Well, you know, if we play this, if this is F and then we bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, bum, that would be below it. That's below it, yeah. And would you say that half of the time that you were playing was down in there below that

F? You know, you'd never play above, Q. See, it's hard if it's a sound, you know, playing an F above. And if you play that above, you see, or C, well then sometimes then you'd play it down below, you see.
Right. But you didn't try to play down low most of the time to take the place of a bass viol or a bass horn or anything.
Why not? Because it really sounds better above after, doesn't it, in most cases.
No, that's right. It sounds much better. I would never try to play too low. I always try to wipe up, you see.
You're closer to the trumpet line, man. Yeah. It sounds better, I suppose.

It sounds better, yeah. Just in some things with the trumpet on low, you know, that's all right. But I notice the boys now playing. They play pretty low sometimes. They play anyway now. They make all of them low, like they make sixteens and faths seconds and all that kind of stuff. That's right. We didn't have enough time, plenty of times, quarters and halves. It wasn't much for the trombone. You had to make your part of it. Like you say you'd syncopate it or something like that and make it sound different than the same bum, bah, bum, bah, like that half and half a quarter. While you'd stick from one and add to the other and everything like that. I see. Or you could sometimes get the slurge, you know, lip white, tongue white. Maybe like that. But that's got a whole lot to do with it too, you know.
